summary: In a holding setting, Arthur and the narrator talk about Dawna Polk, who has them locked up pending brainwashing. Arthur suggests Dawna's aims may partly justify her actions and admits he does things he isn't proud of, while the narrator, shaken, makes a confession about her own ruthlessness. Arthur points out she spared him after knocking him out even though he could have been a threat, and she realizes he is right.
one_line: Arthur and the narrator, held captive pending brainwashing by Dawna Polk, debate morality and the narrator confesses she is not a good person.
key_facts: Arthur says Dawna Polk 'could have worse targets than you and me' if she is really trying to improve things.
The narrator asks what about Courtney, Dr. Kingsley, Reginald Kingsley, and the people in his file.
The narrator asks who gave Dawna Polk the right to choose in the first place.
Arthur says he does 'lots of things I ain't proud of these days' and suspects he won't weigh out well on the scales of judgment.
Arthur says he is not sure he and the narrator would be on the side of the righteous.
The narrator says Arthur 'at least try[s]' while she 'survive[s]'.
The narrator says she doesn't think a whole lot about the people she hurt and that killing a threat has always been the smart thing to do.
The narrator says 'I don't think I'm a very good person.'
Arthur says 'You didn't kill me' and notes she knocked him out and left him alive.
Arthur says 'Yes, I was' a threat and 'you knew I could be.'
The narrator admits Arthur was right, since she had believed she was in the clear.
The narrator notes she felt as if she were making a deathbed confession.
The narrator says the impending brainwashing made frank soul-baring more appealing.
The narrator says Arthur's 'mind was about to get twisted into pretzels, too.'
